description_ru: Выдуманная новость о редком насекомом, найденном в государственном архиве, которое остановило строительство нового здания и озадачило чиновников.
text:
MARLOWE-ON-SEDGE, Eastern Fenlands. A moth no larger than a thumbnail has succeeded where three successive governments, two public inquiries and a determined citizens' committee failed: it has halted construction of the Fenland Regional Archive Extension, a glass-fronted edifice that was to cost forty million crowns and, in the words of its architect, "radiate transparency in a spirit of civic openness." The insect, a pale, unassuming creature identified as the Sedge Ghost Moth, was discovered on the third of October by an archivist who had gone to the basement in search of a stapler.

The archivist in question, Mr Cuthbert Ainsworth-Mbeki, aged fifty-eight, has worked in the building for thirty-one years and is described by colleagues as "a man who has never been known to raise his voice or lose a document." He told reporters that he had noticed a flutter of silvery wings above a stack of tithe maps from the eighteenth century and, being by temperament a cataloguer, had immediately reached for a jar. "I assumed it was one of the ordinary sort," he said. "Then I noticed it was eating the Treaty of Wenlow. Very slowly. And with what I can only call discernment."

The moth was dispatched to the University of Marlowe, where Dr Imogen Falkenrath-Adeyemi, a lepidopterist of considerable reputation and a pronounced fondness for puns, confirmed within hours that the creature was a member of the Sedge Ghost species, previously believed to have been extinct since 1923. "It is," she said, "a lazarus species, which is to say, one that has been declared dead by experts who should have checked the basement." The specimen is believed to be the last surviving population of its kind, a colony of some two hundred individuals, which has lived undisturbed in the archive for a hundred years, subsisting on a diet of parchment, paste and, for variety, the odd ministerial memorandum.

Under the national Habitats Act, the discovery has triggered an immediate injunction against any construction within a radius of three hundred metres. Excavators that had already arrived on the site were obliged to withdraw, reportedly with an air of wounded dignity, and the foundation pit, which had been dug to a depth of nine metres, has been temporarily designated a sanctuary. A sign has been affixed to the fence, informing passers-by that "beyond this point lives a moth of European importance," which has been the subject of several complaints from other moths.

The developers are, understandably, aghast. Mr Roderick Pemberton-Oyelowo, managing director of Glasshouse Civic Partners, said that the company had budgeted for many contingencies, including floods, strikes, and the discovery of a Roman pavement, but "never for a creature that eats our client." He added that the firm's lawyers were examining the possibility of relocating the moth. This idea was swiftly rejected by Dr Falkenrath-Adeyemi, who pointed out that the species had evolved, over a century, to thrive on a particular blend of damp, dust and bureaucratic neglect, "which cannot easily be reproduced elsewhere, except possibly in a ministry."

The affair has also created an awkward situation for the archive itself. A cursory inspection has revealed that the moths have been consuming the collection at a rate of roughly one page in every thousand per year, which, over a century, amounts to a quite substantial loss of local history. The chief archivist, Dame Winifred Thackeray-Osei, has therefore been placed in the uncomfortable position of defending the insects that are devouring her charges. "We are in a delicate position," she conceded. "The moths are protected; the documents are protected; and the law has not yet determined which takes precedence."

Preliminary findings suggest that the moths have a discriminating palate. They are said to prefer eighteenth-century land deeds, to avoid anything written in iron-gall ink, and to be especially fond of correspondence from the Ministry of Drainage, which Dr Falkenrath-Adeyemi attributes to "a particular binding agent in the paste, used in that department, which is irresistible to the species." A few historians have taken a wry satisfaction in the news. One, who has spent a decade seeking a missing planning dispute, remarked that for the first time in his career, he knew exactly where the files had gone.

The wider scientific community has responded with a mixture of delight and mild envy. A professor in another country telegraphed his congratulations and enquired, rather wistfully, whether the archive might require a visiting scholar.

Public reaction has been swift and entertainingly divided. A petition titled Save the Moth has gathered more than forty thousand signatures, while a rival petition, Save the Archive, has managed seven, mostly from archivists. Local schoolchildren have organised a vigil with paper lanterns, which the fire brigade has politely asked them to extinguish, and a pub in the town centre has renamed itself The Ghost Moth, with a new sign depicting an insect of such magnificent proportions that experts have been obliged to remind the public that the creature is, in fact, small and drab.

The mayor, who had campaigned on the promise of the new extension, has adopted a tone of pained diplomacy. "We are, of course, committed to the conservation of our natural and documentary heritage," he said, "and I am confident that a solution can be found that satisfies both." Asked whether the solution might involve a smaller building, he replied that this was "a conversation for the committee," a phrase which, in the Fenlands, is understood to mean that it will be decided in about nine years.

Meanwhile, an interim arrangement has been reached. The archive will remain open, the moths will remain undisturbed and a team of conservators will install climate-controlled cabinets for the most vulnerable documents, an operation expected to cost less than the cost of the foundation pit's fence. Mr Ainsworth-Mbeki, for his part, has been appointed the moth's official guardian, a post that carries a modest stipend and a lanyard. He told reporters he intends to treat the role with the seriousness that it deserves. "After thirty-one years of looking after paper," he said, "it is rather pleasant to be looking after something that wants to be read."

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Рот открыт шире, чем для русского «э»; звук короткий и напряжённый.
Долгий нейтральный гласный: губы не растянуты и не округлены; не «ё».
Тёмный l: кончик языка упирается в дёсны, задняя часть оттянута; не мягкое русское «ль».
Самый частый безударный гласный: короткий, расслабленный, почти неслышный; не произносите его чётко как «а».

questions.question: What did Mr Ainsworth-Mbeki find in the basement?
questions.answer: A rare moth eating the Treaty of Wenlow.

questions.question: Why was construction stopped?
questions.answer: The moths are protected under the Habitats Act.

questions.question: What do the moths prefer to eat?
questions.answer: Eighteenth-century land deeds and old parchment.
